drafts.title: 42.7 miles: the longest fast-charger gap from Denver to Grand Junction is our last stretch
drafts.angle: Denver to GJ is covered every 5 to 20 miles now, except the one stretch locals drive most: Parachute to Grand Junction through De Beque Canyon and Palisade. A hard local number nobody else is posting.
bullets: 54 DC fast-charging locations within 2 miles of I-70 from I-25 in Denver to west Grand Junction, 282 fast ports total (ChargingNear.me, built from DOE AFDC data, updated Nov 10, 2026).
Tesla has 14 of the 54 locations but 158 of the 282 ports, more than half.
Longest gap on the whole run: 42.7 miles, Parachute Supercharger to the Grand Junction Supercharger. Nothing fast in De Beque or Palisade.
Next longest: Glenwood to Rifle 23.9 mi, Gypsum to Glenwood 23.5 mi, Silverthorne/Frisco to Vail about 20 to 22 mi.
Grand Junction end: 9 fast locations, 31 ports (Tesla, Rivian, eVgo, ChargePoint).
drafts.body: 42.7 miles. That's the longest stretch of I-70 from Denver to Grand Junction with no fast charger, and it's our backyard: Parachute to GJ. Where I'd want one: [Palisade / De Beque / ___]. Ever sweat that stretch in winter?
drafts.framework_body:
42.7 miles.

That's the longest stretch of I-70 between Denver and Grand Junction with no fast charger. And it isn't up on the pass. It's right here, Parachute to GJ, through De Beque Canyon and Palisade.

The rest of the mountain is in good shape now. 54 fast-charging stops and 282 plugs between Denver and here, most of them 5 to 20 miles apart. Tesla alone has more than half the plugs.

But the canyon is the hole. In summer nobody cares. In January, with the heat running and a headwind, that 42 miles feels longer. I [plan my stop at ___ / leave Parachute with ___%].

A charger in Palisade would also feed the wineries and fruit stands. That's money staying in our valley.

[photo: me at the Parachute or GJ Supercharger ___]

If you could drop one fast charger between Parachute and GJ, where would it go?

drafts.title: $0: what a real veterans grant costs, and the fake AI one stealing VA deposits
drafts.angle: Not "AI is scary." It's the one-minute family habit that beats it. Veterans Day tie-in: a fake AI-made grant post got veterans to hand over direct-deposit info.
bullets: VA News: a fake "Veterans & Retired Seniors Grant Program" Facebook post, made to look government-sponsored, got veterans to hand over direct-deposit info; some lost thousands in VA payments. VA is working to make them whole.
VA's rule: Stop. Check. Then act. Report VA scams to VSAFE at 833-38V-SAFE (833-388-7233).
Greenville SC police warn of "virtual kidnapping" calls using AI-cloned voices of a loved one and recommend a family code word.
Vox (Nov 6): hang up and call back on the number saved in your contacts, and check how old a social account is.
drafts.body: $0. That's what a real government grant costs to sign up for, and they never need your bank login. A fake AI-made "veterans grant" just stole VA deposits. Our family code word is [___, don't post it]. Does your family have one yet?
drafts.framework_body:
$0.

That's what it costs to sign up for a real government grant. And no real program ever needs your bank login to "send" you money.

Right before Veterans Day, a fake "Veterans & Retired Seniors Grant Program" post on Facebook, made with AI to look official, talked veterans into handing over their direct-deposit info. Some lost thousands in VA payments.

AI didn't hack anybody. It just made the lie look better. The fix is still simple, and it's free:

1. Pick a family code word. Only family knows it. If "your grandson" calls in a panic, ask for it.
2. Hang up and call back on the number already saved in your phone.
3. If it says act now, it can wait.

I told my [dad / brother / wife ___] about this and they said [___].

VA scam line if it happens to you: 833-38V-SAFE.

Does your family have a code word yet?
drafts.ocr_why: Shareable family-safety post with a Veterans Day hook; the code-word question pulls replies and saves from 55+ readers.
drafts.pixel: Kitchen table, talk to camera: "Veterans, a fake grant post is stealing VA deposits. Here are the three things my family does."
drafts.premium_target: Quote VA's official account or a verified veteran creator posting about benefits scams with one line: the code word plus call-back habit.

drafts.title: $30 a month: what one family saved just by charging the EVs at night
drafts.angle: The cheapest EV upgrade costs nothing: charge overnight on a time-of-day rate. Their step two was solar plus a battery that kept Grandma's medical gear running through 46 outages.
bullets: Energy Trust of Oregon (Nov 5, 2026), quoting the family: "We immediately were saving $30 a month on Time of Day just because we charged our EVs at night."
Their battery has covered 46 outages since 2022, from seconds to 7 hours, switching over in under a second.
It kept the heat pump, CPAP, electric lift chair, fridge and medicine running.
Three-generation home, 7 people: 27 kW solar plus 54 kWh battery; the family estimates about $8,000 a year saved on energy, plus no gas.
drafts.body: $30 a month. That's what one family saved just by charging their EVs at night instead of the evening. My overnight rate in Grand Junction: [$___ per kWh]. Are you charging at the cheap hours, or just plugging in when you get home?
drafts.framework_body:
$30 a month.

That's what one Oregon family saved, right away, just by setting their EVs to charge at night instead of the minute they pulled in. Same cars, same driving. They just moved the charging to the cheap hours.

That's the free step. Takes two minutes in the car's app.

Their next step cost real money: solar and a home battery. Since 2022 that battery has ridden through 46 outages and kept Grandma's CPAP, her lift chair, the heat pump and the fridge running. Seven people, three generations, one house.

I'm not telling everybody to go buy a battery. But the night charging part? Everybody with an EV should be doing it.

My rate at night here in GJ: [$___ per kWh]. My car is set to start at [___].

drafts.ocr_why: Dollar opener, a free action anyone can take today, a personal rate fill-in, and an easy yes/no question.

drafts.title: $0 extra: your phone can already explain that confusing bill
drafts.angle: A new AI pendant for older adults reads letters and bills out loud and explains them. Fine for folks who hate apps, but the phone already in your pocket does it today for free.
bullets: Careflick's Oak1 wearable (pendant or clip-on) ships January 2027; reservations open at careflick.com. Price not published.
It explains letters and bills with a built-in camera, books rides and appointments, orders groceries and refills, and works with hearing aids. 15+ languages.
Careflick says it was built from 10,000+ hours of conversations with 1,000+ older adults; family updates only with the wearer's permission, and it asks before doing anything big.

drafts.title: $16 vs $23: Tesla Robotaxi undercuts Waymo on day one in San Antonio
drafts.angle: Price, not tech. A local reporter rode both on launch day and Tesla was cheaper. Plus a smart tip for any rider: check your own uninsured motorist coverage.
bullets: Tesla Robotaxi launched in San Antonio Monday at 5 AM; KSAT's test trip cost $16 vs about $23 on Waymo (Uber about $16).
San Antonio is Tesla's 8th Robotaxi city; launch map about 274 sq mi on paper (Electrek) vs Waymo's 59 sq mi there. Electrek expects 160 to 210 sq mi actually bookable; the airport isn't served.
Austin zone is now 443 sq mi.

A local attorney told KSAT that in Texas the company stands in as the operator when no human intervenes; riders should check their uninsured/underinsured coverage. Terms include arbitration with a 30-day opt-out.
drafts.body: $16 vs $23. A reporter rode Tesla Robotaxi and Waymo on the same San Antonio trip on launch day. Tesla won on price. What I'd pay to skip driving at night: [$___]. Would you ride one, or wait a year?
drafts.framework_body:
$16 vs $23.

A San Antonio reporter took the same trip on Tesla Robotaxi and on Waymo on launch day. Tesla was seven bucks cheaper, about the same as an Uber with a driver.

That's city number 8 for Tesla. Waymo covers about 59 square miles there. Tesla's map is way bigger on paper, though the airport isn't in it yet.

For me this was never about the tech. It's about my folks, and someday me, getting to the doctor or home from dinner at night without having to drive or ask anybody.

One tip from a local lawyer worth stealing: before you ride any robotaxi, look at the uninsured motorist part of your own car insurance.

Not in Grand Junction yet. When it gets here I'd use it for [___]. What I'd pay to skip driving at night: [$___].

Would you ride one now, or wait a year?
